title: Days at or Below Today's Price
statement:
Prices arrive one day at a time. After each new price, report how long the current "good run" is: the number of consecutive days, ending today and counting today, on which the price was less than or equal to today's price.

  • PriceStreak() creates the tracker with no days yet.
  • next(price) records today's price and returns the length of that run.

You only ever see prices from the past, so the answer must be computed as each price arrives.

Tests are a list of operations; the first one creates the tracker. The output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: The second 38 covers 38, 38 and 35, then the 40 stops it. The 50 covers all five days. The 45 covers itself and the 20, then the 50 blocks it.
Equal prices count: the rule is "less than or equal".

hints: The obvious answer walks back through past prices until it finds a higher one. On a steadily rising series, how many steps does that take in total?
Once a day is covered by a later, higher-or-equal price, can it ever be the day that stops a future run?

Keep a stack of [price, span] pairs with strictly falling prices. For a new price, pop every pair with price ≤ today's and add its span to today's span (starting at 1). Push [today, span] and return span.

explain.intuition:
Walking back day by day is O(n) per call, and on a rising series it becomes O(n²) in total. The fix is to notice which past days still matter. If today's price is at least as high as yesterday's, any future day that gets past today also gets past yesterday. So yesterday can be folded into today and forgotten. What remains is a stack of prices that strictly fall from bottom to top, each carrying how many days it has absorbed.

For a new price, pop every stack entry with price ≤ today's, adding up their spans. The entry left on top (if any) is the first higher price, and it stops the run. Each day is pushed once and popped at most once, so the cost is amortized O(1) per call. It is the same trick as "days until a warmer day", just looking backwards and answered online.
steps: Keep a stack of [price, span] pairs.
While the stack is not empty and its top price is ≤ price, pop it and add its span to span.
pitfalls: Popping only on strictly smaller prices. Equal prices must be absorbed too, as the second example shows.
Storing only prices on the stack and computing the span as a count of popped entries. Each popped entry may stand for many days, so you must carry its span (or store the day index).
Forgetting to count today itself: the span starts at 1.

solutions.title: Walk back through every price
solutions.idea: Store all prices. For each new one, walk backwards while the past price is ≤ today's.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack of absorbed days
solutions.idea: Keep prices that strictly fall from bottom to top, each with the number of days it covers. A new price swallows every entry that is not higher than it.

followups: Return the span counting only days with a strictly lower price. Which single comparison changes?
Also answer "how many days until a strictly higher price" for each day, once the whole series is known. Can one pass give both answers?
